title: Ukraine's Largest Drone Maker: Nearly 100,000 a Month, AI Interception Is Just the First Step
dek: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, with interceptor drones costing about $2,000 to shoot down Russian Shaheds worth over $50,000. AI guidance is battle-tested, but full autonomy remains distant.
why: This episode is a rare, direct account from a top Ukrainian drone maker about the real form, cost, and AI limits of battlefield drones. Dense with information, it offers direct value for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers focused on modern warfare, the drone industry, and AI military applications.
skip: You can skip the opening company introduction and jump straight to the middle and later sections on AI and costs.

points.h: Producing nearly 100,000 a month, and still scaling
points.body: Founded in 2023, General Cherry initially made about 10 drones a month; now it produces around 100,000 a month (the exact figure is confidential). The company works with more than 110 military brigades, and the best units burn through over 5,000 drones a month. Production is still ramping up because the battlefield consumes drones at a staggering rate — they have become expendable.

points.h: Hundreds of Ukrainian drone firms, but only 10–15 at the top
points.body: Ukraine may have as many as 2,000 drone companies, but most are garage-sized operations. Only 10 to 15 large firms can produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry claims to be in the top five. This fragmented but vast ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, yet it also means fierce competition.

points.h: AI models built in-house, co-developed with the military
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance system is entirely self-developed, backed by a strong R&D department and close cooperation with military units on the front line. They collect battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This R&D-to-combat-to-feedback loop lets Ukrainian drone tech adapt fast to the changing battlefield, rather than relying on external procurement.

points.h: The rocket-shaped FPV came from Red Bull, not Ukraine
points.body: This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian original; Red Bull first used it for sports events in 2021 or 2022. Ukrainian companies found the shape could reach higher speeds than a standard quadcopter, so they adopted and optimized it. It reflects the Ukrainian drone industry's fast learning and pragmatism — not originality, but effectiveness.

points.h: A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
points.body: General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as the Bullet) cost about $2,000, yet can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is Ukraine's key strategy against Russia's saturation attacks — using cheap drones to exhaust the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding wasting Western-supplied, costly air-defense missiles.

points.h: Interceptors have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drones downed
points.body: General Cherry's tactical interceptor drone (General Trajectory Air) has confirmed over 5,000 Russian drones shot down since production began in February 2025, with more than 1,000 Russian Moniya drones downed in December alone. The Shahed-interceptor model entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills nearing 1,000. These numbers show interceptors have become a significant force in battlefield air defense.

points.h: AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's onboard camera chip, not in the cloud. The operator detects the target via radar, launches the drone, and the AI automatically identifies and locks on without human intervention. This on-device AI avoids battlefield communication delays and jamming, which is key to its real-world viability.

points.h: Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is inevitable
points.body: Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it will be terrifying — killing would no longer require another human, just a robot or drone. Currently they use semi-autonomous AI only on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs would significantly raise costs, making it better to buy more non-AI drones. But he predicts AI technology will spread quickly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.
